propositions.text: Does a superior court justice have jurisdiction to hear judicial interim release applications for young persons charged with s. 469 offences?
propositions.quote: The narrow issue before us is this: does a justice of a superior court of criminal jurisdiction have jurisdiction to hear and adjudicate an application for judicial interim release of a young person charged with an offence listed in s. 469 of the Criminal Code , R.S.C. 1985, c. C‑46 ?

propositions.text: If so, under what circumstances?
propositions.quote: And, if so, (1) under what circumstances?

propositions.text: Is such jurisdiction exclusive or concurrent with designated youth justice court judges?
propositions.quote: and (2) is such jurisdiction exclusive, or is it held concurrently with judges of the designated youth justice court for the province?

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issues: whether superior court justices have jurisdiction for judicial interim release applications for young persons charged with s. 469 offences, under what circumstances, and if jurisdiction is exclusive or concurrent.

propositions.text: T.J.M. is charged with a s. 469 offence and elected trial by superior court judge without jury.
propositions.quote: This appeal is brought by T.J.M., a young person, who was charged with an offence listed in s. 469 of the Criminal Code . The Crown gave notice of its intention to seek an adult sentence for second degree murder, entitling T.J.M. to elect the mode of trial. He elected trial by a superior court judge sitting without a jury

propositions.text: T.J.M. requested a preliminary inquiry and sought judicial interim release before a superior court justice.
propositions.quote: requested a preliminary inquiry, and sought judicial interim release before the application judge, who is a justice of the Court of Queen’s Bench of Alberta.

propositions.text: The application judge found no jurisdiction to grant judicial interim release to a young person, exclusive jurisdiction vested in designated youth court.
propositions.quote: The application judge held that he had no jurisdiction to grant judicial interim release to a young person, finding that Parliament had vested exclusive jurisdiction in the designated youth court for the province

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts that T.J.M. elected trial by superior court judge, sought judicial interim release, but the application judge found no jurisdiction, vesting it exclusively in the youth court.

propositions.text: The court concludes superior court justices have concurrent jurisdiction to hear judicial interim release applications for young persons charged with s. 469 offences.
propositions.quote: I respectfully draw the opposite conclusion: a superior court justice has jurisdiction to hear and decide an application for judicial interim release brought by a young person charged with an offence listed in s. 469 of the Criminal Code . Further, that jurisdiction is held concurrently with the judges of the designated youth justice court for the province.

propositions.text: The court would allow the appeal but make no further order.
propositions.quote: I would therefore allow the appeal, but would make no further order.

propositions.text: Both Crown and appellant agree the appeal is moot due to stay of proceedings but agree the court may hear the merits.
propositions.quote: Both the Crown and the appellant, T.J.M., agree that this appeal is moot, the Crown having entered a stay of proceedings, but say that it is open to this Court to exercise its discretion to hear the merits of the appeal in accordance with Borowski v. Canada (Attorney General), [1989] 1 S.C.R. 342, at pp. 358‑63.

propositions.text: The court agrees it may hear the merits despite mootness.
propositions.quote: I agree.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds superior court justices have concurrent jurisdiction for judicial interim release applications and allows the appeal, noting mootness but agreeing to hear merits.

propositions.text: Section 33(8) YCJA states only youth justice court judges may order release of young persons charged with s. 522 offences, which include s. 469 offences.
propositions.quote: Section 33(8) of the YCJA provides that “a youth justice court judge, but no other court, judge or justice” may order the release of a young person charged with an offence referred to in s. 522 of the Criminal Code . Section 522 incorporates s. 469 offences by reference.

propositions.text: Central issue is identifying who qualifies as a 'youth justice court judge'.
propositions.quote: Central to deciding this appeal, then, is identifying who is “a youth justice court judge”.

propositions.text: The appeal rests on interpreting YCJA provisions about 'youth justice court judge'.
propositions.quote: This appeal therefore rests on the proper interpretation of certain provisions of the YCJA touching on this question.

paragraphs.summary: The court states that only youth justice court judges may order release of young persons charged with s. 469 offences, making the definition of 'youth justice court judge' central to the appeal.

propositions.text: Section 2 YCJA defines 'youth justice court' and 'youth justice court judge' by reference to section 13.
propositions.quote: Section 2 of the YCJA defines a “youth justice court” and a “youth justice court judge” as “a youth justice court referred to in section 13 ” and “a youth justice court judge referred to in section 13 ”, respectively.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes YCJA section 2 defines 'youth justice court' and 'youth justice court judge' by referring to section 13.

propositions.text: Section 13(1) YCJA designates youth justice courts and judges as those established or designated by provinces or councils.
propositions.quote: Section 13 provides, in relevant part: Designation of the youth justice court 13 (1) A youth justice court is any court that may be established or designated by or under an Act of the legislature of a province, or designated by the Governor in Council or the lieutenant governor in council of a province, as a youth justice court for the purposes of this Act, and a youth justice court judge is a person who may be appointed or designated as a judge of the youth justice court or a judge sitting in a court established or designated as a youth justice court.

propositions.text: Section 13(2) deems a superior court judge trying a s. 469 offence without jury to be a youth justice court judge and the court a youth justice court for the proceeding.
propositions.quote: Deemed youth justice court (2) When a young person elects to be tried by a judge without a jury, the judge shall be a judge as defined in section 552 of the Criminal Code , or if it is an offence set out in section 469 of that Act, the judge shall be a judge of the superior court of criminal jurisdiction in the province in which the election is made. In either case, the judge is deemed to be a youth justice court judge and the court is deemed to be a youth justice court for the purpose of the proceeding.

propositions.text: Section 13(3) deems a superior court judge trying a s. 469 offence with jury to be a youth justice court judge and the court a youth justice court for the proceeding.
propositions.quote: Deemed youth justice court (3) When a young person elects or is deemed to have elected to be tried by a court composed of a judge and jury, the superior court of criminal jurisdiction in the province in which the election is made or deemed to have been made is deemed to be a youth justice court for the purpose of the proceeding, and the superior court judge is deemed to be a youth justice court judge.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains YCJA section 13 designates youth justice courts and judges, and deems superior court judges trying s. 469 offences with or without jury as youth justice court judges for the proceeding.

propositions.text: Section 13(1) designates provincially established youth justice courts and their judges.
propositions.quote: Section 13(1), therefore, designates as a youth justice court “any court . . . established or designated by . . . [the province] as a youth justice court”, and designates as a youth justice court judge “a judge sitting in [the] court established . . . as [the] youth justice court”.

propositions.text: Sections 13(2) and (3) apply when a young person elects trial by judge with or without jury under s. 67 YCJA.
propositions.quote: Sections 13(2) and (3) apply where any of the three circumstances described in s. 67 of the YCJA as triggering a right to election apply, and the young person elects to be tried by a judge with or without a jury.

propositions.text: For s. 469 offences, a superior court judge has jurisdiction when the young person elects trial in superior court with or without jury.
propositions.quote: In the case of a young person charged with a s. 469 offence, a judge of the superior court will have jurisdiction when the young person elects a trial in the superior court of criminal jurisdiction sitting without (in the case of s. 13(2)) or with (in the case of s. 13(3)) a jury.

propositions.text: Section 67(2) YCJA gives three trial options for s. 469 offences: provincially designated youth court judge, superior court judge alone, or superior court judge with jury.
propositions.quote: when a young person charged with a s. 469 offence is put to an election, s. 67(2) of the YCJA gives the young person three options: (1) a trial before a s. 13(1) judge of the court designated by the province as a youth justice court; (2) a trial before a judge of the superior court of criminal jurisdiction, who is deemed by s. 13(2) to be a youth justice court judge, sitting alone; and (3) a trial before a judge of the superior court of criminal jurisdiction, who is deemed by s. 13(3) to be a youth justice court judge, sitting with a jury.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains section 13 designates youth justice courts and judges, and that s. 67(2) YCJA gives young persons charged with s. 469 offences three trial options including superior court judges deemed youth justice court judges.

propositions.text: A young person must be tried before a youth justice court judge, whether provincially designated or superior court judge deemed as such.
propositions.quote: The critical point is this: irrespective of the mode of trial elected, the YCJA requires that a young person be tried before a youth justice court judge.

propositions.text: Superior court judges deemed youth justice court judges under s. 13(2) or (3) are deemed so 'for the purpose of the proceeding'.
propositions.quote: And in the latter two instances ... the superior court is so deemed “for the purpose of the proceeding”.

propositions.text: The meaning of 'for the purpose of the proceeding' is the next issue to consider.
propositions.quote: It is to the meaning of that statutory text that I now turn.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds young persons must be tried before youth justice court judges, including superior court judges deemed so for the proceeding, and will now interpret 'for the purpose of the proceeding'.

propositions.text: What procedural steps fall within 'the proceeding' as used in s. 13(2)?
propositions.quote: If a superior court justice is deemed, by s. 13(2), a youth justice court judge “for the purpose of the proceeding”, what procedural steps fall within “the proceeding”?

propositions.text: The application judge concluded 'the proceeding' refers only to the trial.
propositions.quote: The application judge concluded “the proceeding” refers only to the trial.

propositions.text: T.J.M. argues 'the proceeding' has broader application including judicial interim release applications.
propositions.quote: T.J.M. argues that it has broader application, and that it governs his application for judicial interim release.

propositions.text: The court agrees 'the proceeding' includes any step after election to be tried at superior court, including pre-trial judicial interim release applications.
propositions.quote: I agree; the scope of the term “the proceeding”, as it is used in these two sections, is not confined to the trial. Rather, ... it includes any step taken by a youth justice court judge after the young person elects to be tried at the superior court, including any pre‑trial application for judicial interim release.

paragraphs.summary: The court poses the issue of what 'the proceeding' includes, notes the application judge's narrow view, T.J.M.'s broader view, and agrees with the broader interpretation including pre-trial steps.

propositions.text: The term 'the proceeding' is not defined in YCJA and must be interpreted by statutory interpretation principles.
propositions.quote: The term “the proceeding” is not defined in the YCJA . The resolution to this issue therefore lies in the principles of statutory interpretation, by which the statutory text is to be read in its grammatical and ordinary sense, and understood in the context of the entire statute and in harmony with the statute’s schemes and objects.

paragraphs.summary: The court states 'the proceeding' is undefined in YCJA and must be interpreted using statutory interpretation principles.

propositions.text: Caselaw shows three approaches to interpreting 'the proceeding' in ss. 13(2) and (3).
propositions.quote: The caselaw reveals three different approaches having variously prevailed.

propositions.text: First approach equates 'the proceeding' narrowly with the trial, giving exclusive jurisdiction to designated youth court judges for judicial interim release.
propositions.quote: The first ⸺ which the application judge adopted ⸺ proceeds narrowly, equating “the proceeding” with the trial. ... leaving a s. 13(1) youth justice court judge ... with exclusive jurisdiction over the judicial interim release of young persons charged with s. 469 offences, irrespective of the mode of trial elected

paragraphs.summary: The court notes caselaw shows three approaches, the first equating 'the proceeding' narrowly with the trial, giving exclusive jurisdiction to designated youth court judges.

propositions.text: Second approach views 'the proceeding' as including steps after committal to superior court, with exclusive jurisdiction transferring then.
propositions.quote: A second approach ... understands “the proceeding” as including every step taken after the young person is committed to stand trial or arraigned before the superior court of criminal jurisdiction. ... once the jurisdiction transfers to the superior court, the jurisdiction is exclusive.

propositions.text: This approach relies on s. 67(7) YCJA that 'the proceedings shall be conducted' in the trial court after committal.
propositions.quote: This reads “the proceeding”, as it appears in ss. 13(2) and (3), together with the direction in s. 67(7) of the YCJA that, after the young person is committed to stand trial ... “the proceedings shall be conducted” in the trial court.

propositions.text: Cases supporting this approach include Protection de la jeunesse, R. v. B.W.H., and R. v. N.M.
propositions.quote: see Protection de la jeunesse ⸺ 177486, 2017 QCCS 5165, at paras. 34‑35 (CanLII); R. v. B.W.H. (2005), 198 Man. R. (2d) 264 (Prov. Ct.), at paras. 37‑38; R. v. N.M., 2010 MBPC 45, 257 Man. R. (2d) 207, at paras. 45‑55

paragraphs.summary: The court describes a second approach viewing 'the proceeding' as including steps after committal to superior court, transferring exclusive jurisdiction then, supported by cases and s. 67(7) YCJA.

propositions.text: Third approach views 'the proceeding' broadly as any step after election to superior court, with exclusive jurisdiction for superior court judges.
propositions.quote: Finally, a third approach views “the proceeding” as referring broadly to any step in the prosecution. ... This approach has been coupled with the view that the jurisdiction granted to that judge is exclusive.

propositions.text: Cases supporting this approach include R. v. W. (E.E.), R. v. B. (J.), and R. v. F. (M.).

paragraphs.summary: The court describes a third approach viewing 'the proceeding' broadly as any step after election to superior court, with exclusive jurisdiction for superior court judges, supported by cases.

propositions.text: The first two narrow approaches are incorrect; 'the proceeding' has a broader ordinary meaning.
propositions.quote: In my respectful view, the first two approaches cannot be correct. The ordinary and grammatical meaning of the term “the proceeding” is not so narrow.

propositions.text: Black’s Law Dictionary defines 'proceeding' as an act or step part of a larger action or the entire lawsuit progression.
propositions.quote: Black’s Law Dictionary (11th ed. 2019), by B. A. Garner, at p. 1457, defines “proceeding” as “[a]n act or step that is part of a larger action” or “[t]he regular and orderly progression of a lawsuit, including all acts and events between the time of commencement and the entry of judgment”.

propositions.text: No text in s. 13 suggests 'the proceeding' means only the trial; Parliament uses 'trial' elsewhere when intended.
propositions.quote: And no text in s. 13 remotely suggests that “proceeding”, as it appears in ss. 13(2) and (3), refers to anything other than the entire process of a criminal prosecution after the young person elects to be tried at the superior court. ... had Parliament intended to confine the operation ... it would have used the term “trial”, as it did in several other provisions of the YCJA

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the first two narrow approaches incorrect, citing Black’s Law Dictionary and noting Parliament uses 'trial' when intending to limit scope, so 'the proceeding' means the entire prosecution process after election.

propositions.text: Parliament intended superior court justices deemed youth justice court judges to be so for all steps after election until trial.
propositions.quote: The better view, then, in light of the ordinary and grammatical sense of the term “the proceeding”, is that Parliament intended superior court justices who are deemed youth justice court judges by operation of ss. 13(2) and (3) of the YCJA to be so deemed for the purpose of all steps taken after the young person charged with a s. 469 offence elects a trial in the superior court, until trial.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds Parliament intended superior court justices deemed youth justice court judges to have jurisdiction for all steps after election until trial.

propositions.text: The court is not persuaded by arguments relying on reading ss. 13(2), (3) with s. 67(7) YCJA.
propositions.quote: I am not moved from this view by the argument that relies on reading ss. 13(2) and (3) together with s. 67(7).

propositions.text: Section 67(7) directs that after committal, 'the proceedings shall be conducted' in superior court.
propositions.quote: To recount, s. 67(7) directs that, where a young person charged with a s. 469 offence is committed to stand trial at the conclusion of a preliminary inquiry, “the proceedings shall be conducted” (or, in the French version, “le procès” (“the trial”)) in the superior court.

paragraphs.summary: The court rejects arguments relying on reading ss. 13(2), (3) with s. 67(7), noting s. 67(7) directs proceedings after committal be conducted in superior court.

propositions.text: The difference between singular 'proceeding' and plural 'proceedings' is not significant; Interpretation Act allows singular/plural interchange.
propositions.quote: I note, first, that nothing of significance turns on the use of the plural “proceedings” in s. 67(7) and the singular “proceeding” in ss. 13(2) and (3). Indeed, the Interpretation Act , R.S.C. 1985, c. I‑21 , directs that words expressed in their singular form in an Act are to be read as including the word’s plural form, and vice versa (s. 33(2)).

propositions.text: Parliament did not intend s. 67(7) to define the scope of 'the proceeding' in ss. 13(2) and (3) or YCJA generally.
propositions.quote: Parliament cannot, in my view, reasonably be taken as having intended its reference to “the proceedings” (or “le procès”) in s. 67(7) to define the scope of “the proceeding” in ss. 13(2) and (3) or in the YCJA generally.

propositions.text: Interpreting s. 67(7) to limit 'the proceeding' would render other YCJA references to 'proceedings' nonsensical.
propositions.quote: Ascribing significance to its use in s. 67(7) to limit the scope of the term “the proceeding” in ss. 13(2) and (3) would render at least some of those other references to “the proceedings” in the YCJA nonsensical.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the singular/plural difference is insignificant and Parliament did not intend s. 67(7) to limit 'the proceeding', as that would make other YCJA references nonsensical.

propositions.text: Section 20(1) YCJA contemplates proceedings before a justice other than plea, trial or adjudication.
propositions.quote: s. 20(1) of the YCJA states that “[a]ny proceeding that may be carried out before a justice under the Criminal Code , other than a plea, a trial or an adjudication, may be carried out”.

propositions.text: Section 26(9) YCJA states failure to give notice does not affect validity of proceedings, subject to s. 26(10).
propositions.quote: s. 26(9) of the YCJA states that “failure to give a notice [to the young person’s parents] . . . does not affect the validity of proceedings under this Act”. This is subject to s. 26(10), which provides that failure to give such notice does invalidate “subsequent proceedings” unless ...

propositions.text: Interpreting 'proceedings' as only trial would be absurd and undermine procedural notice purpose.
propositions.quote: Interpreting “proceedings” (or “the proceedings”) here to mean only the trial would be absurd in light of the reference to “subsequent proceedings”, and would undermine the purpose of this provision, which is to preserve the validity of procedural steps already taken, while ensuring that the young person’s parents have notice of all further procedural steps to be taken in the prosecution of their child

paragraphs.summary: The court cites YCJA provisions showing 'proceedings' includes steps other than trial, and limiting it to trial would be absurd and undermine notice purposes.

propositions.text: Section 67(7) grants exclusive jurisdiction to s. 13(1) youth justice court judges to conduct preliminary inquiries.
propositions.quote: s. 67(7) vests exclusive jurisdiction in “the youth justice court [judge] referred to in subsection 13(1)” to conduct a preliminary inquiry.

propositions.text: If superior court judges could not acquire jurisdiction until trial, s. 67(7) reference to s. 13(1) would be unnecessary.
propositions.quote: If, however, a superior court judge who is deemed to be a youth justice court judge could never acquire jurisdiction until the trial, it would not have been necessary for Parliament to make specific reference to s. 13(1) in s. 67(7).

propositions.text: Parliament is presumed to avoid superfluous or meaningless words in legislation.
propositions.quote: Parliament is presumed to avoid “superfluous or meaningless words, phrases and larger units such as paragraphs, sections and parts of a legislative scheme” (Bristol‑Myers Squibb Co. v. Canada (Attorney General), 2005 SCC 26, [2005] 1 S.C.R. 533, at para. 178).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes s. 67(7) grants exclusive preliminary inquiry jurisdiction to s. 13(1) judges, and if superior court judges had no pre-trial jurisdiction, the reference would be superfluous, which Parliament avoids.

propositions.text: Section 13(2) deems superior court judge a youth justice court judge for the proceeding; s. 13(3) deems judge without qualification.
propositions.quote: Section 13(2) deems a superior court to be a youth justice court and deems a superior court justice to be a youth justice court judge for the purpose of the proceeding. But while s. 13(3) also deems a superior court to be a youth justice court for the purpose of the proceeding, it deems a superior court judge to be a youth justice court judge without qualification.

propositions.text: Interpreting 'the proceeding' as only trial creates anomaly between s. 13(2) and s. 13(3) judges' jurisdiction.
propositions.quote: Interpreting “the proceeding” to mean only the trial proper would, therefore, create an anomalous situation whereby a superior court justice who is deemed by s. 13(3) to be a youth justice court judge would have jurisdiction ... while a superior court judge deemed by s. 13(2) ... would not.

propositions.text: Parliament could not have intended such a result based on jury presence alone.
propositions.quote: Yet, the only distinction between the two is that at trial the former sits with a jury, and the latter sits alone. Parliament could not have intended such a result.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds that interpreting 'the proceeding' narrowly creates an anomaly between s. 13(2) and s. 13(3) judges' jurisdiction, which Parliament could not have intended.

propositions.text: Decide if superior court judge's jurisdiction over judicial interim release after election is exclusive or concurrent with youth justice courts.
propositions.quote: it remains to decide whether that jurisdiction is exclusive, or whether it also continues to vest in the courts designated by the province as a youth justice court

propositions.text: Caselaw is divided on whether jurisdiction is exclusive or concurrent.
propositions.quote: the caselaw is divided (see, for example, Protection de la jeunesse, at paras. 34‑35; B.W.H., at paras. 37‑38; N.M., at paras. 45‑55; W. (E.E.), at paras. 14 and 21; B. (J.), at paras. 1‑20 and 32; F. (M.), at paras. 46 and 49‑51)

paragraphs.summary: The court states the issue is whether superior court jurisdiction over judicial interim release is exclusive or concurrent, noting caselaw is divided.

propositions.text: Argues superior court's jurisdiction is exclusive based on s. 522(1) of the Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: The argument that a young person’s election to be tried before a superior court judge triggers the superior court’s exclusive jurisdiction ... is grounded in s. 522(1) of the Criminal Code

propositions.text: Section 522(1) states only superior court judges may release accused before or after trial order.
propositions.quote: It states that “no court, judge or justice, other than a judge of or a judge presiding in a superior court of criminal jurisdiction . . . may release the accused before or after the accused has been ordered to stand trial”

propositions.text: This would oust jurisdiction of s. 13(1) youth justice court judges to hear judicial interim release applications.
propositions.quote: Standing alone, this would appear to oust the jurisdiction of a s. 13(1) judge of the provincially designated youth justice court to hear and decide the application for judicial interim release

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues s. 522(1) grants exclusive jurisdiction to superior court judges for judicial interim release, excluding youth justice courts.

propositions.text: Section 522 is subject to s. 28 of the YCJA, which allows YCJA to prevail if inconsistent with Part XVI of Criminal Code.
propositions.quote: section 522 is subject to the caveat in s. 28 of the YCJA , which states that the provisions of Part XVI of the Criminal Code apply ... except to the extent that they are inconsistent with or excluded by [the YCJA ]

propositions.text: Part XVI governs detention and release of young persons unless YCJA provides otherwise, in which case YCJA prevails.
propositions.quote: Part XVI of the Criminal Code governs matters of detention and release of young persons unless the YCJA provides otherwise, in which case the YCJA prevails

propositions.text: Section 33(8) of YCJA confers exclusive jurisdiction on youth justice court judges to release young persons charged with s. 522 offences.
propositions.quote: s. 33(8) of the YCJA confers exclusive jurisdiction (“no other court, judge or justice”) upon “a youth justice court judge” to release a young person from custody

paragraphs.summary: The court explains s. 522 is subject to YCJA s. 28, which grants exclusive jurisdiction to youth justice court judges under s. 33(8) for release of young persons.

propositions.text: Section 13(1) YCJA designates youth justice court judges including provincially designated youth justice court judges.
propositions.quote: ss. 13(2) and (3) of the YCJA deem a superior court judge to be a youth justice court judge, s. 13(1) also designates as a youth justice court judge a judge sitting in the court established by the province as the youth justice court

propositions.text: Section 33(8) YCJA applies to all youth justice court judges without qualification, including s. 13(1) judges.
propositions.quote: It does not qualify the term “youth justice court judge” so as to include only those superior court justices deemed under ss. 13(2) and (3) to be youth justice court judges

propositions.text: Section 522's exclusive jurisdiction provision is inconsistent with s. 33(8) YCJA and does not apply to s. 13(1) youth justice court judges.
propositions.quote: it is inconsistent with s. 33(8) and does not apply

paragraphs.summary: The court finds s. 33(8) YCJA applies to all youth justice court judges, making s. 522's exclusive jurisdiction inconsistent and inapplicable to s. 13(1) judges.

propositions.text: Both superior court justices and provincially designated youth justice court judges have concurrent jurisdiction over judicial interim release applications.
propositions.quote: the jurisdiction is concurrent, and not exclusive to either of them

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes jurisdiction over judicial interim release is concurrent between superior court and youth justice court judges.

propositions.text: Parliament intended YCJA to provide enhanced procedural protections and less formal, expeditious proceedings for young persons.
propositions.quote: Parliament’s intention when enacting the YCJA was to provide young persons with enhanced procedural protections ... and to create less formal and more expeditious proceedings

propositions.text: Concurrent jurisdiction introduces flexibility absent in adult criminal justice, aiding young persons especially in rural areas.
propositions.quote: Parliament would have sought to introduce a measure of flexibility ... particularly significant for young persons in rural areas

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Parliament intended YCJA to enhance protections and flexibility, supporting concurrent jurisdiction for young persons.

propositions.text: Jurisdiction over judicial interim release after trial start is not decided here and left open for future consideration.
propositions.quote: Whether it must be brought before the trial judge ... is a question that I need not decide here, and I am content to leave it open for another day

paragraphs.summary: The court leaves open the question of jurisdiction over judicial interim release after trial start for future cases.

propositions.text: The appeal is allowed; the application judge had concurrent jurisdiction with youth justice court; no further order as appeal is moot.
propositions.quote: I would allow the appeal. The application judge had jurisdiction ... As the appeal is moot, no further order is necessary. Appeal allowed

paragraphs.summary: The court allows the appeal, confirming concurrent jurisdiction and making no further order as the appeal is moot.
